question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question names the best-of-5-games-11 format, so the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0 clause for that format governs: alt-best-of-5-games-11:8.1.3 states players change ends at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game. This differs from the general Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) clause laws-8.1.3 (change in the third game at 11 points), which is the alternative to this clause and does not apply to this format. No other part of the question needs a source.
answer.answer: In the best-of-5-games-11 format, you do not switch ends during the third game at a particular score; per the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0 (in force 2027-01-04), format best-of-5-games-11, Clause 8.1.3, "Players shall change ends: at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game". The general Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) rule that players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points" is the alternative to this clause and does not apply to your format.

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens when the opponent shouts 'fault!' during your stroke. itto-5.9.1.4 directly covers a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, classifying it as deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. laws-13.4.5 makes deliberate distraction by shouting a fault under Law 13.4, so the fault is against the opponent. laws-7.3 states the side winning a rally adds a point and wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault, so the point goes to you. All parts are covered; no part is missing.
answer.answer: Your opponent's shout of 'fault!' while you were making your stroke is a fault against your opponent: a player calling 'fault', etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is considered a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.4), and deliberately distracting an opponent by any action such as shouting is a fault under Law 13.4 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 13.4.5). Because the opposing side committed a fault, your side wins the rally and adds a point to your score (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 7.3: "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a 'fault'").

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play may stop for a bleeding cut, and (2) who may come on court to help. Part 1 is answered by itto-5.14.2 (delay until bleeding stops/wound dressed/Referee advises otherwise), itto-3.6.1.4 (Referee resolves well within a few minutes; disqualification warning if exploiting), itto-5.14.1 (no treatment causing undue delay; Umpire times the delay), and itto-3.6.1.2 (quick relief such as a bandage allowed, no time-consuming treatment outside intervals). Part 2 is answered by itto-3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons on court, same consideration for the opposing side), itto-5.14.1 (Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required), and itto-3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called). All parts have sources, so refused is false.
answer.answer: For your partner's bleeding cut, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise [itto-5.14.2]. The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned, and the Referee may point to potential disqualification if it is suspected that the player is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play [itto-3.6.1.4]. No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court, and the Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury [itto-5.14.1]. The Tournament Doctor may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals [itto-3.6.1.2]. As for who may come on court: the Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, and in fairness the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration [itto-3.6.1.3]. The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court [itto-5.14.1], and when called by the Umpire in case of injury, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court [itto-3.6.1.1].

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: what happens to the match when the court becomes unplayable mid-game, and what happens to the score. itto-5.11.3 covers suspension when a court or its immediate surroundings is temporarily not playable; laws-16.3.1 and laws-16.3.3 cover suspension by the umpire and the effect on the score; itto-5.11.4 covers the suspension call/notation; itto-5.11.5 covers resumption and the score call. No part is missing.
answer.answer: If the dripping water makes the court or its immediate surroundings temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee and play is suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.3: “If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.”). When play is suspended, the Umpire calls “Play is suspended” and notes “S” (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.4: “When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.”). For your score, the existing score stands and play resumes from that point (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 16.3.3: “If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.”). When play resumes, the Umpire notes the suspension duration, ensures you and your opponent are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play” (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.5: “When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.”). The umpire may suspend play when necessitated by circumstances not within the players’ control (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 16.3.1: “When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.”).

citations.quote: If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.
When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: what the umpire can do when the opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. itto-5.9.1.6 directly covers a player throwing sweat/contaminating the court and says Law 16.7 is applied if necessary. laws-16.7.1 and its subclauses state how the umpire administers a Law 16.6 breach (warning, fault if previously warned, fault for flagrant offence), and laws-16.7.2 states the consequence after faulting (report to Referee; Referee may disqualify). No part is missing.
answer.answer: For your opponent as the offending side, Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.6 says that a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. Under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.7.1, the umpire shall administer a breach of Law 16.6 by issuing a warning to the offending side, or by faulting the offending side if previously warned, or by faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach. Under Law 16.7.2, on faulting your opponent under Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3, the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question has three parts: (1) what the line judge does when unsighted — itto-8.5 and itto-8.8; (2) who decides and what is called — itto-2.5, itto-5.8.3, laws-17.6.6, laws-14.2.6; (3) what happens to the rally — laws-14.1, laws-14.3, laws-15.3. All parts are covered by sources, so refused is false.
answer.answer: The line judge must immediately tell the Umpire: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5), and "UNSIGHTED" is one of "The approved hand signals" (Clause 8.8). "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision" (Clause 2.5), and "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call" (Clause 5.8.3) — "Out" if the shuttle landed outside the line, or the score / "Service over" and then the score if it landed "in" (Clauses 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.2). The Laws likewise say that where an appointed official is unsighted the umpire shall "carry out that official's duties or play a 'let'" (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 17.6.6). If no decision can be made, it is a let: "It shall be a 'let', if: a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision" (Law 14.2.6), and "When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called" (ITTO Clause 2.5). A let halts play — "'Let' shall be called by the umpire... to halt play" (Law 14.1) — and the shuttle is not in play when "a 'fault' or a 'let' has occurred" (Law 15.3). For the rally itself: "When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again" (Law 14.3), so the rally is replayed from the same service with no point scored.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during the match. itto-5.12.2 directly answers this: coaches must be seated and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals under Law 16.2. laws-16.2.1 and laws-16.2.2 describe those permitted intervals (60 seconds when the leading score reaches 11, and 120 seconds between games), which confirms the exception but does not change the general prohibition. answer.answer: No. Your coach must remain seated in the designated seat and must not stand court-side during the match, except during the permitted intervals: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (except Handicap matches), and not exceeding 120 seconds between games. (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2; Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clauses 16.2.1 and 16.2.2.)

answer.answer: For a plastic (non-feathered) shuttle, the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, require that "Measurements and weight shall be as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6", and the weight in Law 2.2.6 is that "The shuttle shall weigh from 4.74 to 5.50 grams"; however, "because of the difference in the specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials in comparison with feathers, a variation of up to 10 per cent shall be acceptable", so your plastic shuttle may weigh from 4.74 to 5.50 grams, with up to 10 per cent variation acceptable (that is, roughly 4.27 g to 6.05 g by simple arithmetic). question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: Part 1 (point cost now): itto-5.17.10 directly covers misconduct before "Play" is called — any card given has no effect on the score of the match, but is taken into account if further offences occur during the match, linking to Law 16.7.1.2 (faulting the offending side if previously warned). Part 2 (record after the tournament): itto-5.17.2 requires the Umpire to record and report any misconduct to the Referee, and itto-3.7.3 requires the Referee to send a report on yellow and red cards to BWF (or CC) immediately after the tournament, which may trigger further sanctions. Both parts are answered by sources; refused stays false.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost your opponent a point now. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.10 (in force 2025-04-26), misconduct before the match while on the Field Of Play before "Play" has been called is treated as in Instructions 5.17.3, 5.17.4 or 5.17.5, and "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)" — and under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 16.7.1.2 (in force 2025-04-26), the umpire faults the offending side only "if previously warned", so the card matters only if your opponent commits a further offence during the match, in which case his side is faulted. As for after the tournament: yes, the card is recorded and reported. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.2 (in force 2025-04-26), the Umpire must "Record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken", and under Clause 3.7.3 (in force 2025-04-26), "The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions." So the yellow card goes into the post-tournament report to BWF (or CC) and may trigger further sanctions.
